events.text: Above the morning-sun slope, where the paulownias grow, the mountain goes up into a bare ridge of grey granite with nothing on it but lichen and wind. From the top you can see eleven ranges, one behind another, each paler than the last. You do not know why you came up here. Your throat knows. Every dawn now it fills with a song that is not for the sunrise and not for yourself.
events.arc: The Call on the High Ridge

choices.text: Sing it, at the first grey light, as loud as it will go

effects.log: The song goes out over the eleven ranges and does not come back. A herd boy on the slope below drops his switch and stands with his mouth open until the sun is up.

choices.text: Sing it softly, to learn its shape first

effects.log: It is a strange song. It stops in the middle, as if waiting for something, and then goes on. You do not know yet what it is waiting for.

choices.text: Sit on the ridge in silence and listen to the ranges

effects.log: Wind, a hawk a long way off, water somewhere. No song. You sit until noon. Tomorrow, then.

events.text: A whole year of dawns on the ridge. Frost on the granite in winter, so that you slide on landing; rain in summer, so that the song goes out wet and heavy and falls into the first valley. Nothing answers. The farmers below set their day by you now: when the bird on the ridge sings, it is time to go out to the paddies.
events.arc: The Call on the High Ridge

choices.text: Keep on. Every dawn, whatever the weather

effects.log: Every dawn. In sleet, in fog so thick you sing into a wall of white. The farmers say you are more reliable than the temple bell, which is cracked. (-5 health)

choices.text: Try another ridge, further east

ok.log: A higher ridge, a wider view, a colder wind. Something far to the south-east might have been an echo. Might not. You come back to your own ridge, but the east stays in your ear.

fail.log: The eastern ridge belongs to a pair of eagles, who explain this to you at length and with their feet. (-6 health)

choices.text: Rest for a season. A song sung every day can wear thin

effects.log: A season among the paulownias, eating seed and saying nothing. When you go back up, the song is fuller, as if it had been growing while you were away.

events.text: The mountains have learned your song. You sing, and a breath later the first range sings it back, and then the second, fainter, and the third, until eleven ridges are singing your own voice to you, each a little more tired. It is the loneliest sound you have ever heard. It sounds exactly like an answer, and is not one.
events.arc: The Call on the High Ridge

choices.text: Stop in the middle of the song, so you can tell the echo from anything else

effects.log: You stop where the song stops. The echoes stop too, one by one, obedient. Now if anything sings on in the silence, you will know it is not the mountains.

choices.text: Sing against the echoes, a round, until the whole sky is full

effects.log: Eleven ranges of you. In the valleys people come out of their houses and look up, and an old woman says the sky is having a festival. You feel enormous, and nobody answers.

choices.text: Fly down and sleep in the paulownia. The ridge can sing itself

effects.log: You sleep. In the morning the ridge is silent. The mountains only sing when you do. Of course they do.

events.text: {npc}, a woodcutter on the slope under the ridge, has learned your song. Not well. {He} whistles it through {his} teeth while splitting pine, with the stop in the middle in the wrong place, and the village children whistle it after {him}. Today {he} climbs to the foot of the ridge with a rice ball in a leaf, sets it on a rock, and calls up: "Bird! Whoever you are waiting for, I hope they come. Eat something."
events.arc: The Call on the High Ridge

choices.text: Sing the song once properly, for {him}, from the ridge

mem.note: sang for me from the ridge

effects.log: You sing it once, slowly, with the stop where the stop goes. {npc} stands with the axe in {his} hand and listens all the way through. From then on {he} whistles it right, and so, in time, does the whole valley.

choices.text: Leave the rice ball. A phoenix eats only bamboo seed

effects.log: The rice ball sits on the rock for three days. A crow takes it on the fourth. {npc} comes up, sees the empty leaf, and is delighted. You decide not to correct {him}.

choices.text: Eat the rice. It was kindly meant

effects.log: Rice, and a little salt, and the woodcutter's hands. It sits in your crop like a stone. You were not made for it. You are glad you did it, and sorry, both at once. (-5 purity)

events.text: Dawn. You sing, and stop in the middle where the song stops, and the eleven ranges stop with you. And in the silence, very far, beyond the last pale ridge, something sings on: the second half of your song. Not an echo. An echo is your own voice coming back. This is your song coming back the other way round, in a voice you have never heard and have always known.
events.arc: The Call on the High Ridge

choices.text: Sing the first half again, and wait

effects.log: You sing. The far voice answers. You sing. It answers, nearer. By noon it is three ridges off; by evening there is a second long tail on the paulownia branch beside you, and two shadows on the pond below. The other half of your name.

choices.text: Fly toward it, ridge by ridge, singing as you go

ok.log: You meet in the air over the sixth range, both singing, both out of breath, and nearly fly into each other. Neither of you says anything for a long time. Then you fly home together, and the mountains, for once, are quiet.

fail.log: You fly the wrong way down a valley and lose the voice for a whole terrible day. At dusk it finds you, perched on a dead pine, sulking. It had been following you. (-5 health)

events.text: The first morning in the same tree. Your mate is exactly as tall as you, exactly as bright, and holds their head a little to the left, which you find you have been waiting your whole life to see. Neither of you knows how to begin. Phoenixes do not have a custom for this. There has never been anybody to teach one.
events.arc: The Other Half of Your Name

choices.text: Preen a feather on their neck that is out of place

effects.log: One blue feather, lying the wrong way. You put it right. Your mate holds very still while you do it, and then puts one of yours right, which did not need it. That is how it begins.

choices.text: Show them your paulownia, your spring, your ridge

effects.log: A whole day's tour. Your mate looks at everything politely and drinks from the spring and says, at the end, that their own spring was sweeter. It is the first thing they ever say to you. You are not offended. You are enchanted.

choices.text: Say nothing. Sit beside them and watch the sun come up

effects.log: The sun comes up. Neither of you moves. A farmer below, going out to the paddy, looks up and sees two birds in one tree and goes home again to tell everybody, and forgets to do any work that day.

events.text: Your first duet, on the high ridge at dawn. You sing your half; your mate sings theirs. They come in too early. You go on too long. In the middle both of you sing at once, and the eleven ranges throw back a noise like two cats in a sack, and a whole flock of crows leaves the valley in protest.
events.arc: The Other Half of Your Name

choices.text: Laugh, and start again

effects.log: A phoenix laughing is a strange sound. Your mate makes it too. You start again, and it is still bad, and it does not matter.

choices.text: Insist you were right: they came in early

effects.log: They did come in early. You say so. Your mate says nothing at all for two days, which is how you learn that being right is a very small thing to have.

choices.text: Stop singing your half, and listen to theirs alone

effects.log: Alone, their half is beautiful, and it has its own stop in the middle, where your part goes. You hear the gap your voice is meant to fill. Tomorrow you will try to fit it.

events.text: A morning in late spring, warm, no wind. You sing your half, and stop, and your mate comes in exactly in the stop, and goes on, and stops, and you come in. The two voices go out over the ranges, answering, and the mountains do not echo, because there is nothing for them to add. In the paddies below everybody has straightened up.
events.arc: The Other Half of Your Name

choices.text: Sing it again, the same, so you both remember

effects.log: Again, and again. By the third time it is not luck any more. Below, an old farmer takes off a straw hat and holds it against the chest, the way one does for a funeral, or for the king.

choices.text: Change it a little the second time, and see if they follow

ok.log: You turn the tune; your mate turns with you, as if you had planned it. It is the first time you know, without asking, what the other one will do.

fail.log: You change it; they do not follow; the duet falls apart into the cats-in-a-sack noise again. But the first time was real. Nobody can take the first time away.

events.text: You notice it slowly. Your mate gathers seed all day in the groves, as you do, and puts it in the store, as you do, but eats only what you have gathered. Never their own. They are watching, you realise, to see whether you will share, or count.
events.arc: The Other Half of Your Name

choices.text: Share without counting. Let them eat what they like

effects.log: You stop counting. The store goes down a little faster, and your mate stops watching, and one evening eats a seed of their own gathering, and looks at you, and you both understand that a test has been passed.

choices.text: Ask them, plainly, what they are doing

effects.log: "Seeing," your mate says. "My mother's mate counted." That is all they will say. You did not know there had been other phoenixes. You did not know there were mothers. You have a great deal to learn about the other half of your name.

choices.text: Eat only what they gathered, in turn, and see who gives up first

effects.log: For a whole season each of you eats only the other's seed. Nobody gives up. In the end you both laugh, and the store is exactly where it started.

events.text: You fly low over a still lake at sunrise, the two of you, wingtip to wingtip, and the water below shows two shadows under one stretch of sky. A fisherman in a reed boat sees the shadows before he sees the birds, and then looks up, and nearly goes in the lake.
events.arc: The Other Half of Your Name

choices.text: Fly a second circle, lower, for the fisherman

effects.log: He tells it in every market for years: two shadows on the water, then two birds, so low he could have touched the tails with his pole. He never touched them. He says so, every time, as if it were the important part.

choices.text: Rise high, out of sight, before more humans see

effects.log: Up into the morning, until the lake is a coin. The fisherman will say he dreamed it. It is better, sometimes, to be dreamed.

choices.text: Land on the far shore and drink, together

effects.log: The lake is not a sweet spring, but the stream that feeds it is. You drink side by side. Two reflections. Your mate looks at the water for a long time, as if counting.

events.text: Below your paulownia the village has a quarrel. One of you is the bong, they agree; the other is the hwang. The headman says the bigger is the bong. The schoolteacher says the brighter. The miller's family says it is the one on the left, always, and the blacksmith says to catch the bong is good luck and the hwang bad, so it matters. They go on for a month. Nobody asks you.
events.arc: The Other Half of Your Name

choices.text: Sit on the left one morning, and on the right the next

effects.log: The village nearly comes to blows. The miller's family has to admit that the left one has changed, which is theologically very difficult for them. The children decide it is a game, and are the only ones who are right.

choices.text: Let them argue. It is not their business

effects.log: They argue for a generation. In the end the village splits into a bong end and a hwang end, which hold separate festivals. You go to neither.

choices.text: Look at your mate. Does it matter to you?

effects.log: Your mate looks back at you. Neither of you says which. Neither of you ever will. The question goes down into the village, where it belongs, and you sit in the tree, two halves of one name, and the name is enough.

events.text: Many years together now. You know how they wake, which branch they prefer, the small noise they make when the spring is colder than they expected. You have never asked them which half of the name they are, and they have never asked you. You realise, on an ordinary morning, that you are not going to.
events.arc: The Other Half of Your Name

choices.text: Keep the question unasked, for ever

effects.log: Some things are not a secret. They are just not anybody's business, not even yours. The two of you sing at dawn, and the song does not care.

choices.text: Start to ask, and stop

effects.log: You open your beak. Your mate looks at you. You close it again, and they make the small noise they make at a cold spring, which you have learned is a laugh.

events.text: The pair needs a nest, and a nest needs a tree. There are three you could trust. A daughter's tree in a farmyard, planted the year a girl was born, broad and young. An old scholar's tree beside a schoolhouse, planted to call a phoenix that never came. And a wild paulownia on the morning-sun slope that belongs to nobody at all. Your mate waits for you to choose, which is a way of choosing.

choices.text: The daughter's tree, in the farmyard

effects.log: The farmyard is noisy and the tree is young and in a few years they will cut it for a wedding chest. Your mate points this out. You build there anyway. The girl of the house looks up every morning and waves.

choices.text: The scholar's tree, by the schoolhouse

effects.log: The scholar is very old and very poor and has waited for a phoenix for forty years. The first morning there are two. The scholar sits down in the doorway and cannot get up for a while.

choices.text: The wild tree on the slope, which belongs to nobody

effects.log: Nobody planted it, so nobody will cut it. The wind is worse up here. Your mate likes the wind. You learn to.

events.text: Weaving. Paulownia twigs for the frame, bamboo leaf for the lining, the down from your own breasts for the cup. It takes a whole autumn. Your mate weaves clockwise. You weave the other way. The nest, as a result, has a seam down the middle like a badly mended jacket.

choices.text: Weave their way. It is only a nest

effects.log: Clockwise, then. It feels wrong for a month and then it feels like the only way there ever was. The seam stays, a little ridge in the cup between the two places you each sleep.

choices.text: Keep weaving your way. The seam is honest

effects.log: Two directions, one nest, a seam down the middle. It holds through the first storm better than any nest has a right to. Your mate says it is because of the clockwise half. You say nothing, kindly.

choices.text: Take the whole thing apart, and weave it together from the middle out

ok.log: From the middle, both at once, each pulling the other's strand. It is slow. It has no seam. It is the best nest in the province, and nobody but the two of you will ever see it.

fail.log: Half the autumn gone and the nest is a heap of twigs in the fork. Frost comes. You sleep on the heap, cold and cross, and weave it again in the spring. (-4 health)

events.text: The first quarrel about sticks. Your mate has brought a stick. It is a beautiful stick, straight and pale, and it is from a coffin-maker's yard, and it smells of lacquer and of the dead. You will not have it in the nest. Your mate will not take it out.

choices.text: Take it out yourself, while they are at the spring

effects.log: They come back and see the gap and say nothing. For a week the two of you sleep at opposite ends of the seam. Then one morning they bring a new stick, plain, from a grove, and put it in the gap, and that is the apology, and it is yours too.

choices.text: Let it stay. It is their half of the nest

effects.log: The stick stays. You sleep beside it. It smells of lacquer all winter. In the spring your mate takes it out, quietly, without being asked, and never mentions it. Neither do you.

choices.text: Ask why this stick

effects.log: "Because it was going to be burned," your mate says. "It was a good stick and they were going to burn it." You look at the stick for a long time. You put it in the very bottom of the nest, where it will hold everything up.

events.text: The first winter together. Snow on the paulownia, and the nest a round of warmth in the fork. The seed store is under the bark of the tree, enough for two if neither of you is greedy. At night the wind comes over the ridge and the branch moves, and your mate's long tail is folded round both of you.

choices.text: Sleep. The winter can do what it likes

effects.log: You sleep the deepest sleep of your life. In the spring you wake to find your mate already up, sitting on the edge of the nest, watching you. "You snore," they say. It is the kindest thing anybody has ever said to you.

choices.text: Keep watch, so they can sleep

effects.log: All winter you sleep in snatches and watch the dark. Nothing comes. In the spring you find out that your mate was watching too, every night, so you could sleep. Neither of you slept. Both of you are very pleased. (-3 health)

choices.text: Sing, very softly, the duet with the stop in the middle

effects.log: Under the snow, too quietly for the ridge to hear. In the farmhouse below a child wakes and says there is music in the tree, and is told it is the wind, and knows better.

events.text: You have a place now. On the morning-sun slope, below the ridge, in the oldest paulownia, you sing to the sunrise every day of the year. The sun comes up red out of the eastern ranges as if it had been called. The villages have a name for you, and it is not one you chose.

choices.text: Sing to the sun as if it were listening

effects.log: It comes up red, and redder, and gold. Perhaps it is listening. Perhaps it is only the sun. Either way it comes up, every day you sing, and that is a kind of answer.

choices.text: Sing with your mate, so the sun has the duet

effects.log: Two voices to the sunrise on the paulownia slope. In the valley a temple bell rings late because the monk forgot to ring it, listening.

choices.text: Sing only on clear mornings, and keep the grey ones for silence

effects.log: On clear mornings, the song. On grey mornings, silence, and people in the valley say, "No bird today: it will rain." They are nearly always right, because of you.

events.text: {npc}, a painter of folk pictures, climbs the slope at dawn with a roll of mulberry paper, a box of colours ground from earth and stone, and a lunch {he} forgets to eat. {He} paints for the markets: tigers and magpies, carp, peonies, the red sun and the bird. {He} has painted the red sun and the bird a hundred times and never seen the bird. Today {he} sits down under your tree and opens the box with shaking hands.

choices.text: Sing, and hold still, so {he} can see

effects.log: {npc} paints until the sun is high, and the picture is wrong, and {he} knows it, and paints another. By noon there are seven sheets drying on the rocks. None of them is right. {He} has never been so happy.

choices.text: Fly off. A picture is a kind of cage

effects.log: {npc} paints the empty branch instead, with the sun behind it. It sells better than any bird. People like to imagine.

choices.text: Come down and look at {his} colours

effects.log: Cinnabar, malachite, azurite, an ochre from the riverbank, a soot black. Five colours. {npc} holds very still while you look at them, one by one, as if you were choosing. You touch the blue with your beak. {He} keeps that pot all {his} life and never uses it.

events.text: {npc} comes back every spring now. The trouble, {he} explains to the tree, is that there are two of you, and the picture should have two, a pair under the red sun, everyone knows that; but every time {he} paints the second bird the first one goes wrong. {He} has torn up a whole season of paper. The pile of torn sheets under your tree is the most colourful thing in the province.

choices.text: Sit so close together that {he} can paint you as one shape

mem.note: sat close as one shape for my painting

effects.log: One shape, two tails, two heads turned toward each other. {npc} paints it in one breath and sits back and laughs out loud. It is still wrong. It is less wrong.

choices.text: Let {him} paint only one, and see what {he} does with the second

effects.log: {npc} paints one bird, beautifully. Then {he} paints the second only as a tail, coming in from the edge of the paper, the rest of it out of the picture. {He} looks at it for a long time. "That is right," {he} says. "That is how it is."

choices.text: Shed a feather onto the paper

mem.note: let a feather fall on my painting

effects.log: A red feather spins down onto the wet colour and sticks. {npc} does not dare move it. The painting goes to a market in the capital with a real phoenix feather in it, and nobody believes that either.

events.text: {npc} is old. {He} is carried up the slope now, in a chair on two poles, by two of {his} apprentices, who think this is foolish and do it anyway. {He} has one painting left in {him}, {he} says. The red sun, the paulownia, the five-coloured cloud, and the bird. {He} asks the tree, politely, whether the bird would mind singing one last time.

choices.text: Sing the whole morning song, for {him}

effects.log: {npc} paints with {his} eyes closed. The apprentices say afterwards that it is the best thing {he} ever did, and nobody can paint like it again, though every market painter in the land will copy it for three hundred years: the red sun, the paulownia, and the bird singing.

choices.text: Sing the duet, with your mate, so the picture has both

effects.log: {npc} hears two voices and paints two birds at last, facing each other under the red sun. {He} puts down the brush and says, "There." The apprentices carry {him} down the slope. {He} sleeps all the way.

choices.text: Come down and sit on the arm of {his} chair

effects.log: The apprentices drop the poles. {npc} does not paint at all. {He} sits with the bird on the arm of the chair and watches the sun come up, and says it is a better picture than any {he} made.

events.text: A small hill kingdom lies in the valley under your ridge: a walled town of wooden halls, a few hundred paddies, a lord with a fine hat and a short reign. One morning the lord's men come up the ridge with poles and coils of hemp, and by evening there are nets hung from pine to pine across every saddle of the ridge. You count them. There are a hundred.

choices.text: Fly over the nets, high, and look down at the town

effects.log: From above the nets are grey threads in the pines, a hundred of them, cleverly hung where a bird would cross. In the lord's hall, below, the lamps burn late. Somebody has a plan.

choices.text: Leave the ridge for a season, until they lose interest

effects.log: A season away, in a strange tree. When you come back the nets are still there, mended, and men sit by them all day, playing a game of pebbles on a board scratched in the dirt.

choices.text: Land on a net pole in full view, and look at the net-men

effects.log: Twenty men drop their pebbles and stare. One of them runs down to the town. Nobody tries to catch you. They do not know how. Yet.

events.text: You listen from the eaves of the lord's hall. The lord's geomancer, a thin person with a compass board and a bad cough, is explaining. The kingdom's luck is a phoenix's luck: the mountain is shaped like a nesting bird, and the phoenix on the ridge is its life. As long as it stays, the kingdom stays. If it flies, it falls. So it must not fly. "A hundred nets," says the geomancer. "One for every year of the reign you deserve, my lord."

choices.text: Stay on the eaves and hear all of it

effects.log: The lord does not want to cage you. The lord wants to keep you, which is worse, because it is love of a kind. You fly home in the dark, and the hundred nets look different now: not a trap, a plea.

choices.text: Shake the eaves until the geomancer's compass falls off the table

effects.log: The compass board clatters across the floor and spins and points at the lord. The geomancer turns white and says it is a very good omen. The lord is not convinced, but the nets stay up.

events.text: Dawn on the third day of the spring winds. You fly out to the ridge for the morning song, and your mate takes the low saddle, as they always do, and in the grey light a net is there where none was yesterday. A thrash of five colours in the hemp. Twenty men running uphill with poles. Somebody shouts, "Bong japatda! We caught the bong!" and somebody else shouts, "Fool, it's the hwang, that's bad luck!"

choices.text: Dive at the net-men, between them and your mate

ok.log: You come down out of the sun on twenty men, all wings and five colours and noise. They scatter. Your mate tears out of the loosened hemp and the two of you go up together, leaving long feathers in the net for the lord to keep. (-6 health)

fail.log: A pole across the wing; a second net over your back; you tear out of it bleeding and they have your mate in a cage before you can turn. The cage goes down the ridge to the lord's hall. Two shadows on the slope, and then one. (-28 health)
fail.deathCause: beaten down by a hill-lord's net-men on the ridge

choices.text: Sing, the loudest you have ever sung, so the whole valley comes out

ok.log: The whole valley comes up the ridge: farmers, the miller, the schoolteacher, children. Nobody will cage a phoenix in front of the whole valley. The net-men let the hemp go slack and look at their feet, and your mate goes free.

fail.log: The valley comes out, and stands at the bottom of the ridge, and watches the cage go into the lord's hall. They cannot stop a lord. They only weep, and argue about bong and hwang.

choices.text: Wait for the night. A net-man sleeps; a cage has a latch

effects.log: You watch them carry your mate down the ridge in a bamboo cage and do not move, because moving now would put you in a cage too. It is the hardest thing you have ever done. Night, then.

events.text: The lord has hired a champion to guard the ridge: {npc}, a fighter from outside the kingdom with a net in one hand and a knife in the other, very quick, very quiet, sleeping in the open by the nets with {his} back to a pine. The net-men are afraid of {him}. You watch {him} for a month. {He} cuts {his} rice cake in two every evening and leaves half on a rock, for nobody.

choices.text: Land on the rock where the half rice cake is, while {he} watches

effects.log: {npc} does not reach for the net. {He} looks at you a long time and says, "They told me it was for the luck of the kingdom. They did not tell me you would look at me." That night the net stays rolled at {his} feet.

choices.text: Keep out of {his} reach. A champion is a champion

effects.log: You keep to the far side of the ridge. {npc} keeps the nets. Neither of you crosses the other. It is almost a kind of respect.

choices.text: Drop a long feather on {him} while {he} sleeps

mem.note: let a feather fall on me in the night

effects.log: In the morning {npc} finds the feather on {his} chest. {He} looks up the ridge, and puts it inside {his} jacket, and does not report it to the lord.

events.text: Night over the hill kingdom. A hundred nets on the ridge, a cage in the lord's hall, and in the cage the other half of your name, silent for the first time since the high ridge. The moon is down. The hall has a back court, a latch of bamboo, two guards who drink barley tea to stay awake and are losing.

choices.text: Go in by the smoke hole, and open the latch with your beak

ok.log: Soot, a beam, a dark room that smells of lacquer and fear. The latch gives. Your mate does not make a sound until you are both over the town wall, and then makes the small noise that is a laugh, and does not stop for a mile.

fail.log: A guard wakes. A lamp, a shout, a sword through the smoke hole that takes three tail feathers and some of you with them. By the time you are clear of the roof, the cage has gone down the south road under guard, and you never learn where. (-25 health)
fail.deathCause: cut down in the smoke hole of a hill-lord's hall

choices.text: Cut the nets on the ridge instead, all hundred, in one night

effects.log: Beak and claw, a hundred nets, one after another until your mouth bleeds. At dawn the lord comes out and sees the ridge bare and understands: the bird would sooner die than be kept. The cage door is opened at noon, with ceremony, and your mate walks out of it as if it had been a short visit. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go up to the ridge where the champion sleeps, and wait

effects.log: The lord's champion wakes and finds you on the rock, looking. A long silence. Then the champion gets up, walks down to the hall, past guards who do not dare, and opens the cage with one hand. By morning the champion is gone from the kingdom, and so is your mate's silence.

events.text: Years after the nets. The hill kingdom still stands, smaller and poorer than its lord hoped. The geomancer is dead; the lord is old. Every spring the lord climbs the ridge alone, without a single man, sits under your pine and says to the empty branches: "I only wanted you to stay."

choices.text: Come and sit in the pine above the old lord, this once

effects.log: The lord looks up and sees you and covers their face with both hands. You stay until the sun is high. The kingdom has a good year, and nobody can say why.

choices.text: Stay away. Being kept is not the same as staying

effects.log: You sing on the far ridge, where the lord can hear but not see. The lord listens, and understands that this is the most that will ever be given, and goes home, and burns the last net pole for firewood.

events.text: The champion on the ridge turns, one evening, and for a moment you know the shape of that stance from the inside: the net in one hand, the lord's coin in the sleeve, the weight of a bird pulling against the hemp. You held a net like that once, on a ridge like this, in a life with hands. You held it for the lord. You remember the bird's eye.

choices.text: Forgive the one who held the net

effects.log: It was you, and it was a long time ago, and the bird in the net looked at you exactly as you are looking at this champion now. You let it go. The champion, below, feels something lift and does not know what.

choices.text: Land on the champion's rock, so this one chooses differently

effects.log: The champion looks up at you for a long time and lowers the net. You do not know whether it was the bird or the memory that did it. Neither does the champion.

events.text: A knife through hemp: you hear it in the dark on the ridge, and something in you answers before you know why. Once, in a life with hands, you were hired to hold a net like these, and on the third dawn you cut your own net and let the bird go, and the lord's men turned on you. You still remember the weight going out of the hemp.

choices.text: Cut one net tonight, for that human

effects.log: One net, at the saddle where your mate flies. It falls in a grey heap. The net-men find it in the morning and blame each other. Somewhere a debt between lives is a little lighter.

choices.text: Sing on the ridge at dawn, for the one who was beaten

effects.log: The song goes out over the hundred nets. Nobody below knows who it is for. You do.

events.text: You know how this ends, because you ended it once. A night, a knife, a hundred nets, a human running along the ridge in the dark cutting every one of them, and in the morning a bare ridge and a lord who understood. That human was you. The ridge seems to remember too: the old pines lean the way they leaned that night.

choices.text: Cut the nets the way that human did, all of them, in one night

effects.log: Beak instead of a knife, wings instead of feet. The same ridge, the same order, saddle by saddle. At dawn the lord comes out to a bare ridge for the second time in two lives, and sits down on the ground. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let the lord learn it without you, this time

effects.log: Every lord learns it in the end. You watch from the far ridge and wait. It takes this one eleven years.

events.text: A southern kingdom, old and tired, its king fond of banquets and its ministers fond of land. A stranger arrives from the north with a compass board and very good manners, and is given a seat in the palace. The stranger tells the king a beautiful thing: the royal city lies in the shape of a phoenix's nest. That is why its luck has lasted a thousand years. But a nest without eggs is a nest the phoenix leaves.

choices.text: Fly to the capital and look at its shape yourself

effects.log: You circle the city from high up for a whole day. It is not shaped like a nest. It is long and narrow between two rivers, pointed at one end. You have seen this shape before, on the river, carrying rice to market.

choices.text: Ignore it. Humans have told stories about you before

effects.log: They have, and they will. You go back to the paulownia. But the word "nest" sticks in you like a seed husk, and in the night you find you are thinking about the southern city.

choices.text: Find the stranger's lodging and watch by night

effects.log: The stranger does not sleep. Letters, by lamplight, and in the small hours a rider takes them north. A geomancer who writes to the north every night is not working for the south.

events.text: The king has believed it. All over the royal city the people are heaping earth into round mounds: in the palace grounds, by the old tombs, in the chestnut grove by an old king's grave, in the market. Baskets of earth on every back, a whole season of farming lost. The mounds rise, grassy and enormous, like eggs. "So the phoenix will never leave," the overseers shout, and the people carry, and do not ask which phoenix, or whether it was ever here.

choices.text: Fly low over the mounds, so the people see a phoenix that is not staying

effects.log: You go over the city at noon and on south without turning. The people stop and point. The overseers shout louder: the phoenix has come to bless the eggs! It is astonishing what an overseer can make of anything.

choices.text: Sit on the largest mound and refuse to sit on it

effects.log: You land, look down at the earth egg, step off it, and go and sit in an ordinary chestnut tree. The children laugh. The children understand. Nobody listens to the children.

choices.text: Leave the kingdom to its own folly

effects.log: It is not your city and they did not ask you. You fly north and sing on your own ridge. The mounds go on rising without you, which tells you everything about whom they were for.

events.text: You knew something was wrong, and now you know what. From the high air on a clear day the royal city between its two rivers is a boat: long, narrow, pointed at the prow, the palace for a cabin. The earth mounds lie all over its deck like rice sacks. A boat with too much cargo, in a current. It sits lower every year.

choices.text: Show your mate

effects.log: Your mate looks for a long time from the high air. "A boat," they say. "And they think they are building a nest." Then, after a while: "We should not be on it when it goes."

choices.text: Circle until you are certain

effects.log: Every day for a month. The city is a boat. The mounds are cargo. The current is the years. You do not know what it means, except that it means something, and that nobody below can see it.

choices.text: Sing over the city a song with no stop in it, a warning

effects.log: A song nobody has heard you sing. People shiver in the market without knowing why, and an old ferryman by the river looks up and says, quietly, "That is the song for a leaking hull."

events.text: Night, in the chestnut grove by the old king's grave, where the most earth eggs stand. The stranger with the compass board is digging. Alone, with a spade, by a covered lantern. A deep hole, then deeper, lined with stones: a well, where no well should be. The digging goes on all night, and at dawn a horse is waiting at the north gate.

choices.text: Wake the city: scream over the grove until the lamps come on

ok.log: Lamps, then torches, then the whole quarter in nightclothes in the chestnut grove, looking into a fresh well. The stranger is gone, but the well is found. They fill it in by noon. Whether it was in time, nobody will know for a hundred years.

fail.log: Lamps come on, and go off again: only a bird screaming in the chestnuts, an omen, very bad, go back to sleep. In the morning there is a new well in the grove and nobody who saw it dug.

choices.text: Follow the stranger north, to see who sent the spade

effects.log: Nine days on the road, a rider and a bird. At the end of it, a young lord of the north in a plain hall, who reads the geomancer's report and says, "So the boat has a hole." You fly home. You have seen what the next kingdom looks like.

choices.text: Let it be done. Kingdoms sink; you are not the ship's carpenter

effects.log: You watch the stranger finish and wash the spade and ride away. A well in a chestnut grove. Water rising in it. You sit until dawn, and you remember the place.

events.text: The southern king sends a delegation up your mountain with gifts: a dish of the finest millet in the kingdom, a jade perch, and an invitation. The earth eggs are ready. The nest is ready. Would the phoenix do the kingdom the honour of coming to live in it, for ever?

choices.text: Refuse, plainly, and stay on your own ridge

effects.log: You do not touch the millet. You do not look at the jade. The delegation waits three days and goes down the mountain, and tells the king the phoenix is considering. The king builds more eggs.

choices.text: Go and sit in the city for one season, out of pity

effects.log: One season on a palace roof in a city that is a boat. The king weeps with joy every morning. The ground under the palace is wet. You leave at the first frost, and the king thinks you will be back. (-5 purity)

choices.text: Lead the delegation to the chestnut grove and stand over the well

effects.log: They follow a bird into a grove and find a well that should not be there, or the place where one was filled. The eldest of them understands at once, goes very quiet, and goes home to tell a king who will not listen.

events.text: Word comes from bird to bird, the way all true news comes: the bamboo of the southern province is in flower. Not one clump. All of it, every grove in three counties, at once, as it does once in a human lifetime, or two. The bamboo-cutters are staring at their stems. The old ones among them have gone very quiet.

choices.text: Fly south at once

effects.log: Three days south on the wind. The first grove you reach is pale with flowers from end to end, and the seed is already falling. You eat until you are ashamed of yourself, and then gather.

choices.text: Finish the season at home, then go

effects.log: You go late. The groves are still in flower, but the rats got there first. Still: more seed in a morning than you find in a year at home.

events.text: The flowering grove. A whole hillside of bamboo gone pale and strange, tassels of flower hanging where no flower has hung for sixty years, and the seed falling with every gust like a fine grey rain. Under the stems it lies ankle-deep. You have never seen so much food in one place. Neither has anything else on the mountain.

choices.text: Gather with your mate for a whole season, side by side

effects.log: From first light to dark, every day, a season long. Two sets of tracks in the fallen seed, crossing and crossing. The store under the paulownia will last for decades. Your mate says it is the happiest season of their life. It is yours too.

choices.text: Gather until you can carry no more, and then gather more

effects.log: You carry seed north in your crop, again and again, a dozen trips, until your wings ache. The store is full. You sleep for a week. (-5 health)

choices.text: Gather enough, and leave the rest for the grove

effects.log: Enough is enough. The rest falls. Some of it, a very little, will root, and in a few years there will be bamboo here again. You will be back for it.

events.text: The rats come. Out of the stone walls and the field-banks and the mountain, more rats than there are stars, fat on the fallen seed, breeding in the warm husks. They climb the stems. They eat the seed on the stalk. They look at you without fear, because there are so many of them.

choices.text: Drive them off the last good grove

ok.log: Wings and noise and five colours. They go, for an afternoon, and you gather the last of the grove before they come back.

fail.log: There are too many. A bitten foot, a torn wing, and the grove is theirs by evening. (-10 health)

choices.text: Leave the groves to the rats. You have enough

effects.log: You fly home with what you have. Behind you the rats eat the groves bare. Then, because rats do not stop, they go looking for something else to eat.

events.text: The flowering is over and the bamboo is dying. All of it, every grove in three counties, yellow and then grey, standing dead on the hillsides. The bamboo-cutters cannot understand it. They blame a curse, a magistrate, a fox. One of them, a young one, sits in the dead grove and weeps, because the grove was the family's whole living.

choices.text: Drop a handful of seed from the store in front of the young cutter

effects.log: The cutter looks at the seed, and up at you, and slowly understands: the bamboo flowered and seeded and died, the way rice does. It will come back from the seed. "Sixty years," says an old cutter behind. "Your grandchildren will cut it." The young one plants the seed anyway.

choices.text: Sit in the dead grove with the cutter a while

effects.log: Neither of you understands the other, but the cutter stops weeping after a while and looks at the five colours in the grey grove, and says, "Well. Something good came of it." You hope so.

choices.text: Fly home. Your harvest is the grove's death; that is how it is

effects.log: You fly home over the grey hills with your store full. That is how it is. You do not like how it is.

events.text: The rats have finished the bamboo seed, and they have moved on to the villages. They come out of the dead groves at dusk in a grey tide and go into the granaries. They eat the rice in the jars and the barley in the bins and the seed rice for next year. In the village under your tree the children are digging for wild roots on the hillside.

choices.text: Watch the granary at night and drive the rats from it

effects.log: Every night for a month you sit on the granary roof and scream when the tide comes. It helps a little. A granary saved by a bird is a story the village tells for a long time. (-6 health)

choices.text: Lead the village children to a hillside of wild yams

effects.log: A bird that flies a little way and waits, and flies a little way and waits. The children follow it to a slope thick with wild yam. They do not go hungry that winter. They never tell the grown-ups how they knew.

choices.text: It is not your rice, and it is not your rat

effects.log: You stay in your tree. The village goes hungry. You did nothing to them, and you know it, and somehow it does not feel like nothing.

events.text: Winter, and the village under your paulownia is starving. What seed you kept from the flowering is under the bark, enough to feed a household for a winter if you are generous. Bamboo seed is grain, and humans can eat it. The house nearest your tree has three children and a grandmother, and the grandmother has stopped eating so the children can.

choices.text: Share the store with that house

effects.log: You break the bark and let the seed spill down into the yard in the night. In the morning the grandmother finds it, and kneels in it, and the house eats all winter. Your store is thin. The lean years will come for you sooner now.

choices.text: Share half

effects.log: Half the store, spilled into the yard. It is not enough for the winter, but it is enough for the grandmother to start eating again. You keep the other half for your own lean years.

choices.text: Keep the store. A phoenix that starves cannot come in peace

effects.log: You keep it. That is not wrong. In spring the grandmother is not there any more, and the children are thinner, and they wave at your tree anyway.

events.text: The famine is over. The rats starved when the seed and the rice were gone, the way rats do, and the village is thinner and fewer and planting again. On the gatepost of the house by your tree someone has painted a bird, badly, in five colours. Under it, in a child's hand, a single word: "seed".

choices.text: Sit on the gatepost beside the painting

effects.log: The children come out and compare. The painted one is bigger. You allow it.

choices.text: Sing in the paulownia, so the house knows you saw

effects.log: The door opens a crack. Somebody inside says, "It saw." Nothing more. It is enough.

events.text: Drums in the capital, and new banners on the walls: the land below has a new ruler. The heralds are out on every road saying that heaven smiles on the reign. You have heard heralds say that before. For the first time in your life it occurs to you that heaven might want to know whether it is true, and that you are the one who would have to go and look.

choices.text: Fly to the capital at once, and watch

effects.log: You find a temple roof across from the palace with a view of the granary gate. You will sit here for a long time. It is the first time you have looked at humans to judge them, and you find you do not enjoy it.

choices.text: Ask your mate what they think of heralds

effects.log: "Heralds," your mate says, "are paid by the year." That is all. But the two of you go to the capital together, and sit on two ends of the same roof.

choices.text: Wait. A reign shows its face slowly

effects.log: A year in the paulownias. The springs below the capital will tell you something by the autumn; the granaries by the winter. You can wait. You are very good at waiting.

events.text: The granary of the capital, from a temple roof across the street. A long tiled storehouse, a gate, a line of people with sacks. You watch for a season. In the spring the gate opens to the poor, and a clerk with a brush writes down every measure. In the autumn the gate opens at night, for carts with no lamps.

choices.text: Follow the night carts

ok.log: Through the dark streets to a minister's warehouse by the river. Not to the palace. The ruler may not even know. That is a thing to learn about rulers: what they do not know is also what they are.

fail.log: A night watchman with a bow takes you for an owl and nearly takes you for supper. You lose the carts. (-5 health)

choices.text: Watch the clerk instead, who writes every measure

effects.log: The clerk writes every measure in the spring, and none in the autumn, and goes home every night looking more tired. You decide you trust the clerk. You do not know yet what that tells you about the ruler.

events.text: The royal prison, outside the west wall: a yard of beaten earth, a long low hall with barred windows, a pillory, a well. You sit in the persimmon tree over the wall for a season and count. Who goes in. Who comes out. Who is carried. In the winter a woman comes every day to the gate with a bowl of rice for somebody inside, and is turned away every day.

choices.text: Count, and nothing else. A witness does not take sides

effects.log: More in than out. Few carried. The woman with the bowl, every day. Numbers are not a verdict, but they are not nothing. You keep them like seed.

choices.text: Drop a persimmon at the woman's feet one cold morning

effects.log: She looks up into the tree and sees five colours, and says nothing, and puts the persimmon in the bowl beside the rice. The next day the guard lets her in. You will never know if that was you.

events.text: The court music. On the feast days the palace orchestra plays in the great courtyard: stone chimes on their frames, bronze bells, the long bamboo flutes, the zithers, the drum. You listen from the roof. Music cannot lie, the old books say; a frightened orchestra plays frightened. Today the flutes are in tune and the drummer is smiling, or the flutes are a hair sharp and the drummer watches the throne. You cannot decide which.

choices.text: Listen through every movement before deciding anything

effects.log: By the last movement you have it: the music is true where the ruler can hear it, and a little false at the far end of the courtyard, where the ministers stand. Something is wrong far from the throne. Or near it, in a way the throne does not hear.

choices.text: Ask your mate what they hear

effects.log: Your mate listens with their head on one side, the left, as always, and says what they hear. You do not agree. You listen again, and you still do not agree, and that is a thing you will have to carry into the courtyard if you ever go down.

choices.text: Hum one true note from the roof, and listen to what answers

ok.log: One note, very soft. The first flute hears it and comes into tune with it without knowing why. The drummer looks up. Nobody else does. You learn more from the drummer's face than from the whole feast.

fail.log: The note is louder than you meant. Every face in the courtyard turns up to the roof. You are gone before they see you, but the court talks of nothing else for a month.

events.text: The night after the dance. You came down into the courtyard at the last movement and stood in the measured dance, and the court saw you, and the ruler wept. Now the palace is dark, and the capital is singing in the streets, and something has come in on your body that was not there yesterday. It does not itch. It is just there, like a name.

choices.text: Look at it in the palace pond by moonlight

effects.log: A pattern on your feathers, like a character written by a brush that was never dipped in ink. You stand over the water a long time. So this is what the old books meant. You are a kind of letter, and this is the first word.

choices.text: Fly home before the court can thank you

effects.log: A court that has been blessed wants to give gifts, and a gift is a perch, and a perch is a cage. You are over the walls before the first lamp is lit. The ruler sends heralds to every mountain. None of them find you.

choices.text: Sit with your mate on the palace roof till dawn, and say nothing

effects.log: Neither of you says it. The land below is going to have years of peace, and you did nothing but stand in a courtyard and be seen. It does not feel like nothing. It feels like the most dangerous thing you have ever done.

events.text: The heralds were on the road before you left the courtyard. Heaven favours the reign! The phoenix came in the dance! In a village three days from the capital you see your own image on a banner, red and gold, over a tax collector's table, and a farmer spits on the ground beneath it.

choices.text: Land on the banner pole, where the farmer can see you are sorry

effects.log: The farmer looks up at a real bird under a painted one. The farmer does not spit again. The farmer does not forgive you either. You did not expect it.

choices.text: Watch the court more closely next time, whatever it costs

effects.log: You go back over everything: the granary, the prison, the music. Where you looked away. Where you wanted it to be true. A phoenix that wants a ruler to be worthy is the most dangerous thing in the land.

choices.text: Fly to a sweet spring and drink until you feel clean

effects.log: You drink until you are cold through. You do not feel clean. You feel cold. It is a start. (-3 health)

events.text: Years into the reign you graced. You fly to the palace spring at dawn, as you sometimes do, to drink where the luck of the land comes up out of the ground. It tastes of iron. Not much. A rusty nail in a bucket. In the courtyard the ruler, grey now, is shouting at a minister, and the music on the feast day was a hair sharp.

choices.text: Drink again, to be sure

effects.log: Iron. No mistake. The reign is turning. You have a few years, the old knowledge in your bones says: leave the land in sight of everyone while the pattern is still bright, or stay and watch it go dull.

choices.text: Tell your mate, and decide together

effects.log: Your mate tastes it and says nothing for a long time. "We came for them," they say at last. "Must we go for them too?" Yes. That is the other half of coming. (Leave the Land before the pattern dulls.)

choices.text: Pretend you did not taste it. The ruler was worthy once

effects.log: You fly home and tell yourself it was a nail in a bucket. It was not. You know it was not. (-2 purity; the reign is declining whether you look or not.)

events.text: Watching the court from the temple roof, you remember a courtyard you have never stood in as a bird: the ninth movement, two birds in the measured dance, and a human, strong enough to see what heaven sees, saying aloud that the king was worthy. You were that human. This ruler has the same way of listening to music as that king had.

choices.text: Trust the old testimony, a little

effects.log: You look for worth, and you find it more easily than you would have. Whether that is wisdom or an old habit you cannot tell. The ruler, below, has a good year, as if someone had believed in them.

choices.text: Watch harder because of it

effects.log: An old word from an old life is not evidence. You watch the granary twice as long. It is the most honest thing you can do with a memory.

events.text: Over the palace at dusk, a memory that is not a bird's: a courtyard, the ninth movement, two birds who turned and asked you whether they must stay, and your own human voice telling them about the crime under the throne. Here, now, under this palace, in the cellar under the throne room, you can smell something old and wrong.

choices.text: Find what is under this throne

ok.log: An old cellar, an older ledger, a family of officials who disappeared. Not this ruler's crime; the throne's. This ruler sits on it and knows. You will remember that when you decide.

fail.log: Stone, dust, nothing you can read. But the smell stays in your feathers for a season.

choices.text: Let it lie. That was another court and another life

effects.log: You fly home. Every court has a cellar. You do not have to open every one. You are not sure that is true.

events.text: You remember, very faintly, being asked by two birds in a courtyard whether a king was worthy, and saying it was not for humans to answer. Now you are the bird, and there is nobody to ask. It turns out the question was always going to be yours.

choices.text: Watch for yourself, then

effects.log: The temple roof, the granary, the prison, the music. Three seasons. Nobody to ask but your own eyes. You find you were right, back then: it was not for humans. It was for you.

choices.text: Ask your mate the question you once refused

effects.log: Your mate listens to the whole question, and to the story of the human who would not answer it, and says, "You were wise then, and you are lazy now. Go and look." You go and look.

events.text: Another reign you came down for, years ago, in a measured dance. The ruler is old now, or frightened, or listening to someone new. The springs below the palace taste faintly of iron, and the granary gate opens at night for carts without lamps. You have seen this before. You know what it asks of you.

choices.text: Make ready to leave the land, in full sight

effects.log: Not yet; soon. You fly once over the capital at noon to be sure. Everybody looks up. They are waiting to see what you do. (Leave the Land, before the pattern dulls.)

choices.text: Give it one more season; old rulers have recovered before

effects.log: One more season of iron water. Old rulers have recovered before. Not many. You watch, and drink elsewhere.

events.text: Before you go down into a courtyard, your mate always looks first. This time they look a long time, and turn away. "Not this one," they say. "I do not care what you saw in the granary. Not this one."

choices.text: Trust them, and stay on the roof

effects.log: You stay on the roof. Your mate puts their head under their wing, as if ashamed to have won. Perhaps they are right. You will find out the way everyone finds out, slowly, from the springs.

choices.text: Trust your own watching. Tell them so, gently

effects.log: "I watched for three seasons," you say. "So did I," says your mate. Neither of you moves. The decision is still yours, and it is heavier now than it was. (Come in the Dance, or do not.)

choices.text: Watch one more season, together, before anyone decides

effects.log: One more season, wing to wing on the temple roof. Your mate points out things you missed. You point out things they missed. You still do not agree. You agree a little less badly.

events.text: It has happened four times now. You settle in a valley for a few years, and somewhere near your tree the ground goes soft, and a spring comes up that tastes of sweet rice liquor. The villagers do not know what to make of it. The old ones put a straw rope round it, and a bowl of clean water on a flat stone, and bow.

choices.text: Drink first each morning, so the spring stays sweet

effects.log: It stays sweet. The village washes its babies in it and its dead, and the old ones say it cures coughs, which it does not, and that it is lucky, which it is.

choices.text: Leave the spring to the village and drink elsewhere

effects.log: It is theirs now. You find a spring higher up for yourself. The village spring stays sweet anyway, for a while, out of habit.

events.text: {npc}, the new county magistrate, has heard of the sweet spring. {He} comes with a surveyor and twelve labourers and has a stone wall built round it, with a gate, and a clerk at the gate. The water is now the county's. A jar of it costs a measure of rice. The village women stand in a line with their jars and do not go in.

choices.text: Stop drinking from it. Let it know whose it is

effects.log: You never land on that wall. Within a month the water in the walled spring is flat. Within a season, it tastes of the stones. {npc} has the clerk beaten for watering it.

choices.text: Sit on the gate in full view, so everyone sees whose spring it was

effects.log: The whole village sees you on the gate of the walled spring. So does {npc}. {He} orders a net. You are gone before it comes, but {he} has seen what you are, and decided that you are a thief.

choices.text: Bring the village to the old spring higher up the hill

effects.log: A bird that flies uphill and waits, with jars following. The upper spring is smaller, colder, and free. {npc} sends a surveyor up the hill. The surveyor cannot find it. The surveyor is, as it happens, from the village.

events.text: The walled spring has dried. A crack in the stones, a wet patch, a smell of mud. The clerk at the gate has nothing to sell. {npc} stands in front of it with {his} hands behind {his} back and says, loudly, to the whole yard, that the bird did this. The bird stole the county's water. The bird is a thief, and a bad omen, and must be caught.

choices.text: Let {him} say it. The springs know who walled them

effects.log: Bird-catchers in the hills for a year, paid by the county. They catch a great many pheasants. The village eats well, and says nothing, and goes up the hill for water.

choices.text: Fly over the yard and drop one bamboo seed on {his} hat

effects.log: It bounces off the black gauze into the dust. The whole yard looks at the seed. {npc} goes purple. In the villages they tell it for years: the phoenix paid the magistrate for the water, one seed, which was what it was worth.

events.text: The magistrate who walled the spring is gone, recalled to the capital in disgrace for a different matter entirely. The walls round the dry spring are falling. One spring morning the village children, playing in the ruin, find the ground soft again, and water coming up between the stones. It tastes of sweet rice liquor.

choices.text: Land on the broken wall and drink, so they know

effects.log: The children run for the grown-ups. By noon the whole village is pulling down the rest of the wall with their hands, stone by stone, and nobody tells them to stop.

choices.text: Let them think the spring came back by itself

effects.log: It did, in a way. You only stayed. The village puts the straw rope round it again, and the bowl on the flat stone, and bows.

events.text: The paulownia in the farmyard, the one you have slept in these last seasons, was planted the year the daughter of the house was born. {npc} is seventeen now and talks to you every morning while drawing water: about the weather, the pig, a matchmaker who keeps visiting. This morning {he} stands under the tree a long time and says, "They will cut you after the harvest. For my chest. I am sorry. I wanted you to know first."

choices.text: Sing for {him}, the morning song

effects.log: {npc} stands with the bucket in both hands and listens to the whole song. At the end {he} laughs and cries at once, which humans can do, and goes in to tell nobody.

choices.text: Stay in the tree to the very last day

mem.note: stayed till the tree came down

effects.log: Every morning until the harvest. The axes come on a grey day. You leave the branch when the first blow shakes it and sit on the barn roof and watch it come down. {npc} watches from the doorway. Neither of you looks away.

choices.text: Find another paulownia before the axes come

effects.log: A young tree on the slope behind the village. It is not the same. {npc} sees you go, and understands, and waves a dipper.

events.text: The paulownia is down. The trunk lies in the yard, pale and light as cork, and a carpenter from the next village saws it into boards and stacks them to dry under the eaves. It will be a chest: a nong with brass hinges, for {npc}'s clothes and quilts when {he} goes to the groom's house. You sit on the boards at night. They still smell like your tree.

choices.text: Sleep on the boards until they are made into the chest

effects.log: A whole winter on a stack of planks under the eaves. The carpenter finds a long blue feather between two boards and builds it into the back of the chest, where nobody will ever see it. It seems right.

choices.text: Fly away. It is wood now, not a tree

effects.log: It is wood now. You know that. You fly to the slope, and do not look back at the yard, and look back.

events.text: The chest is finished, and the family has paid a travelling painter to decorate the lid. The painter has never seen a phoenix. Nobody has; that is what phoenixes are for. So the painter paints one from a pattern book: a rooster with a long tail, frankly. Under a red sun, on a paulownia. {npc} looks at it and says nothing politely.

choices.text: Land on the yard wall, where the painter can see you

effects.log: The painter turns, sees you, drops the brush in the dirt. Then picks it up, wipes it, and with shaking hands turns the rooster into something better. Not right. Much better. "Nobody will believe this," the painter says, and is correct.

choices.text: Let the rooster stand. It is a kind thought, badly painted

effects.log: It is a kind thought. Most of what humans do about you is a kind thought, badly painted. You find you do not mind.

events.text: The night before {npc} leaves for the groom's house. The chest stands in the yard, packed. By lamplight {npc} comes out with a brush and the painter's leftover colours and kneels by the lid. There is one bird on it. {npc} paints a second, facing the first, under the same red sun. It is a little crooked. {He} looks up into the dark eaves where you are sitting, and says, "There. Now it is not alone."

choices.text: Sing, very softly, the duet with the stop in the middle

effects.log: Softly, both halves, the way you sing in the nest. {npc} sits back on {his} heels in the lamplight and listens to the end. In the morning the chest goes down the road on a carrier's back, two birds on the lid, one painted by a stranger and one by the bride.

choices.text: Come down and stand beside the chest, once

effects.log: You stand in the lamplight beside the two painted birds. {npc} does not reach out. {He} looks from you to the lid and back, and nods, as if checking the colours. Then you are gone, and {he} sits up all night by the chest, and does not sleep, and is not tired.

events.text: {npc}, the daughter of the farmyard paulownia, the child who talked to your tree, comes home to the village for the spring rites, years after the wedding, with a carrier behind {him} and the wedding chest on the carrier's back. {He} has it set down in the yard where the tree stood, and opens nothing, and only points to the lid. A travelling painter put one bird there, from a pattern book: a rooster, frankly. Beside it, a little crooked, facing it, is a second bird, and you can tell which hand painted that one.

choices.text: Sing the duet with the stop in the middle, for the chest

effects.log: Both halves, softly, from the roof. {npc} sits down on the chest as if {his} legs had decided it, and listens to the end. "I knew one bird was not right," {he} says to nobody. "I knew it."

choices.text: Land on the lid, between the two painted birds

mem.note: stood on my chest between the painted birds

effects.log: Three birds on one lid for the length of a breath. The carrier drops to both knees. {npc} does not. {He} looks at you, and at the second painted bird, and nods, as if checking the colours were right.

events.text: You pass over the capital at dusk, and from the eaves of a minister's mansion something shrieks up at you: "Hsss!" An owl, grey and horned, with a dead rat clamped under one foot. It is the owl of the dead pine. Or it says it is; owls are hard to tell apart, and it has done well for itself. "Mine!" it hisses, covering the rat. "This mansion is mine. This rat is mine. Go away and want something else."

choices.text: "I do not eat rats." Fly on

effects.log: "Everyone wants the rat," the owl tells your back. "Everyone says they do not." You hear it all the way across the city.

choices.text: Land on the far end of the eaves and look at it

effects.log: It puffs up to twice its size and sits on the rat. Behind it, through the window, the minister counts silver by lamplight. The owl and the minister have the same shoulders. You did not know an owl could look like its master.

choices.text: "We have spoken before. Is the rat still good?"

effects.log: The owl freezes. "You remember," it says, as if that were the most suspicious thing of all. "Everyone who remembers a rat wants it." It shuffles round to keep its back between you and the rat, and the minister inside looks up at the noise.

choices.text: "Hsss!" back at it

effects.log: The owl is so astonished that it lets go of the rat, and has to dive off the eaves after it, and comes back with mud on its face. You are halfway to the mountains before you stop laughing.

events.text: The owl has the minister's ear. You hear it from the eaves at night, a dry voice, low, under the sound of the abacus: the phoenix has been seen over the mansion three times. The phoenix wants the minister's post. The phoenix will sit on the palace roof and the king will give the post to whoever the phoenix favours. The minister listens. The minister is the kind of human who would.

choices.text: Stay away from that mansion for good

effects.log: You never fly over it again. It makes no difference. The owl tells the minister that the phoenix is avoiding the mansion, which proves it is plotting.

choices.text: Sit on the minister's own roof at noon, in full view, and eat nothing

effects.log: All afternoon on the ridge-tiles, in plain sight, wanting nothing. The minister comes out and looks at you and goes in again. The owl hisses from the shadows, sitting on its rat, frightened for it. You almost pity it.

events.text: The minister's bird-catchers are on your ridge: three men with lime-sticks, a clap-net, a cage with a decoy pheasant in it, and a bag of millet. They lime every branch of every paulownia within a day's walk. On the slope below, a dish of millet is set out on a flat stone, very white, very fine. The owl watches from a dead pine, rocking from foot to foot.

choices.text: Stay off the paulownias until the rain washes the lime away

effects.log: A month of sleeping in pines and on rocks. Your feet ache and your temper frays. Then it rains for nine days, and the lime runs off the branches in grey threads, and the bird-catchers go home with a great many sparrows. (-6 health)

choices.text: Knock the dish of millet off the stone in front of the owl

effects.log: The millet goes everywhere. The sparrows come down by the hundred. The clap-net comes down on the sparrows. The bird-catchers spend a day letting out sparrows, which is what they deserve.

choices.text: Lead the bird-catchers a long way off, then lose them

ok.log: A flash of five colours on a far ridge, then another further on. They follow for three days over three ridges and end up in a county where nobody has heard of their minister. They decide to stay. The pay is better.

fail.log: A lime-stick on a pine you thought was safe. You tear free with a bare patch on one wing and the bird-catchers holding a fistful of blue feathers. They will sell them for a fortune. (-12 health)

events.text: The owl comes to your ridge, alone, at dusk, with the rat. It sets the rat on a rock between you, very carefully, and steps back. "Take it, then," it says. "Take it and go. I cannot sleep for wondering when you will take it." The rat is very old. It is, you think, the same rat.

choices.text: Push the rat back to the owl with your beak

effects.log: The owl stares at the rat, and at you, for a long time. Then it picks up the rat and flies back to the city without a word. It does not believe you. It will never believe you. But it slept, you hear, that night.

choices.text: Leave the rat on the rock and fly away

effects.log: When you look back the owl is sitting on the rock beside the rat, not touching it, as if it no longer knew whose it was. It is still there at dawn.

choices.text: Tell it what the rat is

effects.log: "It is a rotten rat," you say. "It always was." The owl puts a foot on it, hard. "That is what someone would say," it says, "who wanted it."

events.text: {npc}, governor of the province, wants to send a phoenix to the capital as tribute. It would make {his} name. A cage arrives on an ox-cart: gilded bamboo, a perch of red sandalwood, silk curtains, room for a long tail. It is set up in the governor's courtyard, door open, like an invitation to a banquet. {He} sits beside it every evening and waits, and tells the cage, aloud, how comfortable it is.

choices.text: Look at the cage from a pine, and leave it empty

effects.log: It is a very beautiful cage. You have never seen anything made with so much care for you. That is the worst thing about it.

choices.text: Land on top of the cage, never inside it

effects.log: On the roof of it, not in it, for a whole evening. {npc} holds very still, like a hunter, and you hold still, like a bird that knows. At dusk you go. {He} writes to the capital that the phoenix approves of the cage.

events.text: {npc} has changed tactics. In the cage, on a silver dish, is millet: the best millet in the province, yellow as the sun, hand-picked, every grain the same size. {He} has heard that a phoenix may fly a thousand li hungry. It is a lean year for you. The store under the paulownia is down to husks. The millet smells of summer.

choices.text: Fly a thousand li hungry, then

effects.log: You fly away from the smell of summer with your crop aching. It is a long way to the next bamboo. You make it. The millet is still in the cage when you pass over in the spring, gone grey. (-8 health)

choices.text: Take a single grain from the dish, so {he} knows you could

effects.log: One grain, from the door of the cage, without setting a foot inside. You swallow it and fly. It tastes of nothing you want. {npc} counts the dish all night and finds one missing, and is happy for a week. (-5 purity)

choices.text: Eat. You are hungry, and it is only millet

effects.log: You go into the cage and eat. The door does not close; {npc} is cleverer than that. It will close next time. You fly out full and ashamed, and a sparrow on the courtyard wall looks at you with interest. (-8 purity)

events.text: {npc} has done the cleverest thing yet. {He} has found a sweet spring in a temple in the hills, a real one, that tastes sweet as rice cakes, and had it dug out and piped down the mountain in bamboo to a stone basin in {his} courtyard, beside the cage. The monks are furious. The water is perfect. You can smell it from your ridge.

choices.text: Drink from the temple's own spring, up the hill, where it still trickles

effects.log: A trickle left in the temple yard after the pipe was cut. The monks see you drinking from it and are comforted, and send a petition to the capital about the governor's plumbing that takes eleven years to answer.

choices.text: Break the bamboo pipe, so the water goes home

ok.log: One blow, and the pipe parts at a joint halfway down the mountain, and the water runs back into the old channel. The temple has its spring by evening. The courtyard basin goes dry. {npc} has the pipe mended twice. You break it twice.

fail.log: The pipe is bound with iron at every joint. You hurt your beak and achieve nothing, and the governor's guards see five colours on the hillside. (-8 health)

choices.text: Drink from the basin. The water did nothing wrong

effects.log: It is the sweetest water you have had in a year, and it is stolen, and it tastes stolen. The guards close the courtyard gate behind you, and you have to go over the wall. (-5 purity)

events.text: The tribute road. {npc} has given up on the phoenix and sent the capital a peacock bought from a merchant, with a letter. The court is not fooled. {npc} is recalled. The gilded cage goes up for sale in the provincial market, where a poultry seller buys it for a very large rooster.

choices.text: Fly over the market and look at the rooster in your cage

effects.log: The rooster looks back at you from behind the gilded bars, perfectly content, with a dish of millet and a silk curtain. Somebody in the crowd says, "That is the phoenix," and the poultry seller does not correct them. You fly on, and laugh most of the way home.

choices.text: Let {npc} go without another look

effects.log: A governor recalled; a cage sold; a rooster in silk. It was never about you. It was about a letter to the capital. Most of what humans do near you is.

events.text: A goshawk at the nest. A big hen bird, a falconer's escapee with a bit of leather jess still on one leg, wild three winters and very hungry. It comes out of the grey sky at your mate, who is on the rim of the nest with their back turned, and hits them with both feet.

choices.text: Go at it, beak and wings, before it strikes again

ok.log: Five colours and fury. The goshawk has never been hit by anything its own size from above. It goes, screaming, with a torn tail. Your mate is on the floor of the nest, bleeding from the back. (-10 health)

fail.log: It is quicker than you, and it has done this before. It cuts you across the breast and your mate across the wing before it lets go and goes. Two of you in the nest, bleeding. (-26 health)
fail.deathCause: torn by a goshawk at the nest

choices.text: Scream for the hundred birds of the valley

effects.log: Magpies, crows, a cloud of buntings, all screaming. The goshawk cannot hunt in a cloud. It goes. It took a long time to come. Your mate is lying very still in the bottom of the nest.

choices.text: Drop low through the branches, the way the first goshawk taught you, and come up under it

effects.log: The old scar on your side remembers before you do. Down through the twigs, under the hawk, up into its belly. It has never been hit from below. It goes. Your mate is cut, but less than it could have been.

events.text: A season of nursing. Your mate cannot fly. The wing hangs, and the cuts on the back weep, and they sleep most of the day in the bottom of the nest and pretend not to be frightened. You bring seed, and water from the spring in your crop, one beakful at a time, and sit on the rim, and watch the sky.

choices.text: Never leave the nest. Bring everything to them

effects.log: All season on the rim, flying only to the spring and back. You get thin. Your mate gets better, slowly, and one morning moves the wing on their own, and looks at you, and you both pretend it is nothing. (-6 health)

choices.text: Sing to them every dawn from the rim

effects.log: Your half of the duet, then the stop, and then nothing, because they cannot sing yet. Then, one dawn, a very small sound in the stop, from the bottom of the nest. You do not miss a single dawn after that.

choices.text: Find a healer: the herb-gatherer in the village

ok.log: An old herb-gatherer climbs a paulownia at seventy because a five-coloured bird kept landing on the path in front of them. Moxa, a poultice, a splint of bamboo. "Well," the old one says, coming down, "nobody will believe that."

fail.log: The herb-gatherer thinks you want the herbs, and leaves a bundle at the foot of the tree with a polite bow. It is the wrong bundle. It is the thought that counts, and you carry it up anyway.

events.text: Your mate flies again. Not as before: a little lower on the left, a hitch in the wingbeat when they turn. On the first long flight together they go up to the high ridge, and land, a little hard, and look at you, and wait.

choices.text: Land beside them, a little hard, the same

effects.log: You come down a little hard, on purpose. Your mate knows it was on purpose. Neither of you says so. The duet that morning has a hitch in it on the left, and the eleven ranges sing it back exactly.

choices.text: Sing the morning song with the stop where it always was

effects.log: And into the stop, their half, a little rough. Whole. The farmers in the paddies below straighten up, as they used to. Some things come back.

events.text: The store under the bark is empty. You scrape the hollow with your beak and get husks. There is no bamboo in flower anywhere the birds have heard of, and the winter has a month to run. Your mate looks into the hollow after you, and then at you, and then down at the farmyard, where the hens are pecking yellow millet out of the frost.

choices.text: Fast, both of you, until the thaw

effects.log: A month on the branch, side by side, eating nothing. The cold gets into your hollow bones. Neither of you mentions the millet. At the thaw you fly to the groves together, slowly, like old birds. (-10 health)

choices.text: Peck the millet. A phoenix that dies cannot abstain

effects.log: You go down among the hens. They make room, astonished. The millet is warm and dull and fills you. Your mate stays on the branch and does not watch. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Let your mate give you the last of their own seed
