effects.log: Your mate has kept back a crop of seed, the way you did not think to. They give it to you, all of it, and fast. You eat it, because they will not stop looking at you until you do. In the spring they are thin, and you are ashamed, and they are not.

events.text: The store is empty again. This time your mate speaks first. "I will eat millet," they say. "Only me. Then the last of the seed is yours, and one of us stays clean." They say it very calmly, as if it had been decided some time ago, which it has.

choices.text: Let them. Somebody has to stay clean

effects.log: They go down among the hens every morning for a month and come back up and do not look at you. You eat the last seed, alone, and it tastes of their millet. (-3 health)

choices.text: "Then I eat millet too." Go down together

effects.log: Two phoenixes among the hens. The farmer's child sees it and runs in shouting, and nobody believes the child, which is the only luck you have that winter. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Refuse, and fast. Both of you, again

effects.log: A second fasting winter. Your mate is angry for a week, then too tired to be angry. At the thaw, the first seed you find, you give to them, and they let you. (-10 health)

events.text: Empty again. This time you say it first, before they can: you will eat the millet, and they will have the last of the seed. You have been thinking about it since the last lean winter. Your mate looks at you as you looked at them, and you understand at last how it felt.

choices.text: Do it. Go down to the hens

effects.log: Down among the hens. It is easier than you feared and worse than you thought. Your mate eats the last seed slowly, looking at you the whole time, so that you are not alone in it. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Let them talk you out of it

effects.log: They talk you out of it. You both fast. Somewhere in the second week you both start laughing at the same time, at nothing, out of hunger, and cannot stop. (-10 health)

events.text: Another lean winter, and the old argument, and this time neither of you starts it. You sit on the branch above the empty hollow. Who breaks first, the old question, is not a question any more. Each of you has broken for the other already. What is left is the winter.

choices.text: Fast together, and sing at dawn anyway

effects.log: Thin voices on the high ridge in the frost. Weaker every morning. Still both halves. The farmers below say it is the saddest song they ever heard, and the most stubborn. (-10 health)

choices.text: Fly south together to look for a grove, however far

ok.log: Nine days south, and on the ninth an old clump flowering alone on a riverbank, out of season. Enough. You eat side by side in the snow and do not say a word. (-4 health)

fail.log: Nine days south and nothing. You come home thinner than you left. At least you were together for all of it. (-12 health)

events.text: The store is empty. You are alone on the branch, and the winter is long, and down in the yard the hens are pecking millet, and a sparrow on the fence is watching you with its head on one side. "A phoenix may fly a thousand li hungry," it says. "Who told you that? Was it another phoenix? Was it a full one?"

choices.text: Fly the thousand li, then

effects.log: You fast. The sparrow watches you do it all winter with a kind of horrified respect. In spring it brings you the news of a grove in flower in the south, for nothing, and will not say why. (-10 health)

choices.text: Peck the millet, this once

effects.log: "There," the sparrow says. "Was that so bad?" It was. It was also not. You do not know which is worse. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Drink from the sweet spring until you can bear the hunger

effects.log: Water and nothing. It does not feed you, but it keeps you clean, and clean is a kind of warmth. (-7 health)

events.text: Empty store, cold branch, a mate beside you, and the old lean-year arithmetic: one store, two crops, a winter. You have done this before. You will do it again.

choices.text: Fast together

effects.log: Side by side, eating nothing, until the thaw. It does not get easier. You get better at it. (-10 health)

choices.text: Peck millet, so they can have the last of the seed

effects.log: Among the hens again. Your mate eats the seed and does not thank you, because thanks would make it a debt. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Let them give you their share

effects.log: They give. You take. In the spring they are slow on the wing, and you fly slower beside them, and nobody below notices. (Your mate is weaker for it.)

events.text: A provincial governor below your mountain: stern, honest with money, cruel with debtors. Your mate has watched the office for a year and thinks the governor worthy. You have watched for the same year and think not: you saw the debtors' yard. Your mate saw the granary books. You are both right. You cannot both be right.

choices.text: Hold your ground: the debtors' yard outweighs the books

effects.log: You say it. Your mate says theirs. Neither of you moves. That night, for the first time, you sleep at opposite ends of the branch, and the seam in the nest feels like a wall.

choices.text: Give way. They watched as long as you did

effects.log: You give way, and they know you have not changed your mind, and that is worse for both of you than a quarrel. A quiet winter.

choices.text: Watch together for one more year before anyone says anything

effects.log: One more year, side by side on the gate roof. You show them the debtors' yard. They show you the books. Neither of you is convinced. Both of you are a little less sure.

events.text: A season of the quarrel. The duet at dawn goes on, because neither of you will be the one to stop it, but the stop in the middle is longer now, and colder. The farmers in the paddies have noticed. One of them says the birds on the ridge must have had words. The others tell that one not to be ridiculous.

choices.text: Fill the stop: come in early, on purpose, the way they used to

effects.log: You come in early, the way they did on the first morning. They hear it, and know it, and the next morning they come in early too. It is not an apology. It is the shape of one.

choices.text: Keep the stop as long as it is

effects.log: The silence in the middle of the song gets a little longer every week. The farmers stop arguing about whether the birds have had words.

events.text: Years later, the governor dies, and the truth comes out the way it does, in pieces at the funeral. The books were honest: not a grain missing in twenty years. The debtors' yard was real: three who died in it. Both. The province weeps and curses at the same funeral, and the mourners go home confused.

choices.text: Go to your mate and say you were half right

effects.log: "Half," you say. "Half," says your mate. It is the most honest thing either of you has said in years. The seam in the nest is just a seam again.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let the funeral say it

effects.log: You sit side by side above the funeral road and watch the mourners argue. Nobody below is ever going to agree about this governor. Above, at last, two birds do.

events.text: The apology, when it comes, comes from the one who was less wrong, which is how apologies go between birds who have sung together for generations. A seed, set on the rim of the nest. Not from the store. Found that morning, alone, on a far slope, carried a long way.

choices.text: Eat it, and bring one back tomorrow

effects.log: One seed each way, every morning, for a month. Then you forget to keep count. Then you forget that there was anything to count.

choices.text: Leave it on the rim, and sit beside it

effects.log: The seed stays on the rim of the nest all winter. Neither of you touches it. In the spring it sprouts, a single green thread in the nest, and you both find this very funny.

events.text: The north-east gate of a walled city stands on a wooded hill where every small bird in the province nests. They nest in the gate: in the eaves, the vault, the gatehouse beams. The gate is white with droppings and loud with chicks. A painter has been ordered to put a king of birds on the vault ceiling, to frighten them off, and has come to the hill to find out what a king of birds looks like.

choices.text: Fly through the gate, slowly, under the painter's nose

effects.log: The painter is on a ladder with a brush in the mouth. You go through the vault at walking pace, five colours in the shadow, and out into the sun. The painter drops the brush. The sparrows in the eaves go very quiet.

choices.text: Sit on a beam in the vault for a whole day

effects.log: All day on a beam in the cool of the gate while the painter works below and looks up, and works, and looks up. By dusk there is a bird on the vault ceiling, among clouds. It is not you. It is close enough to frighten a sparrow.

choices.text: Stay on your hill. A painted bird is a lie about a real one

effects.log: The painter paints something from a pattern book. It looks like a rooster. The sparrows nest in its beak.

events.text: A year after the painting. The small birds have gone from the north-east gate: to the woods, the temple, the pine on the hill. Not one nests in the vault. The gatekeepers swear the painted bird's eye follows them. The sparrows, when you pass over, call you names you had not heard before.

choices.text: Visit the sparrows in their new woods and see that they are well

effects.log: They are well. They are furious. They nest in the woods and complain about the gate as if it were a lost kingdom. It was a gate. They were sparrows. They will be fine.

choices.text: Sit on the gate roof once, so the painting keeps its power

effects.log: One morning on the gate roof in plain sight. The whole city comes to look. After that, nobody in the city ever doubts the painting again.

events.text: Something of you went into that paint. You know it on a cold morning, far from the city: a small ache, like a feather pulled, every time a sparrow tries to nest in the north-east gate and sees the bird in the vault and leaves.

choices.text: Let it ache. That is the price of a painted guard

effects.log: A small ache, for as long as the paint lasts. It will last a long time. You find you can carry it.

choices.text: Ask the painter to paint over it

effects.log: You go back and sit on the ladder until the painter understands. A coat of white over the bird. The ache goes. The sparrows come back. You do not feel better. You feel lighter, which is not the same.

events.text: A gate in a damp valley, and the valley is full of centipedes: under stones, in the rice straw, in the sleeves of sleeping children. The villagers have heard that a cock is the centipede's enemy, and that a phoenix is a kind of cock. They have come up the hill with a basket and a great deal of hope. "Please," says their headman, to your tree. "You look just like a rooster."

choices.text: Be insulted, and go anyway

effects.log: You are a phoenix. You are five-coloured, and the old books write virtues on your body, and you look nothing like a rooster. You fly down the valley to their gate in a terrible mood.

choices.text: Refuse. A phoenix does not eat centipedes, or anything but seed

effects.log: The headman goes home with the empty basket. The next week the village buys a rooster, a very large one, and puts it on the gate, and it eats centipedes all summer and grows famous.

events.text: You sit on the valley gate for a season. You do not eat a single centipede: you are a phoenix. The centipedes do not know this. They see a great bird on the gate, like the cock in every story their grandmothers told them, and go, in a long brown line, out of the valley and over the hill.

choices.text: Watch them go, and say nothing to anyone

effects.log: The valley is clean by the autumn. The villagers think you ate them all. You let them. It is, you are learning, much of what being a phoenix is: being believed.

choices.text: Tell the headman, somehow, that you ate none

effects.log: A bird that turns its head away from every centipede the headman holds up. The headman understands at last, and laughs until falling over, and tells the whole valley that the centipedes left out of respect.

events.text: The valley has painted you on its gate, in thanks. The painter has never seen you, only heard you described by villagers who said you looked like a rooster. It is a rooster. A large, proud, very well-painted rooster, with a long tail.

choices.text: Accept it with dignity

effects.log: You sit on the gate beside it, once, so the valley can compare. The valley compares, and decides the painting is a better likeness. You fly home with what dignity is left.

choices.text: Laugh, as a phoenix laughs

effects.log: You laugh until you have to hold on to the gate. The painter, watching from the road, decides the bird is pleased, and paints six more.

events.text: There is a trade in the hill kingdoms that you did not know about until now. Crown-makers set five-coloured feathers into the gilt-bronze crowns of their lords, and the lords pay for the feathers by weight in gold. The men who bring the feathers do not ask where from. This morning, on your slope, you find a long blue tail feather that is not yours, tied with red thread to a stake. Bait.

choices.text: Leave the slope at once

effects.log: You go. Behind you, in the reeds, somebody curses quietly. You will know the smell of them from now on: hemp, pine tar, a little bronze polish.

choices.text: Circle high and find the hunters in the reeds

ok.log: Four of them, flat in the reeds, with clap-nets and a long pole. You go over them at a height they cannot reach and scream once, so they know they are seen. They pack up by noon.

fail.log: You go too low. A pole catches your tail. You leave three feathers in a hunter's fist and go up bleeding. Three feathers is a year's wages. They will be back. (-10 health)

events.text: The feather-takers have a new trap. A clearing in the pines at dawn, and in it, set on poles in a ring, polished bronze mirrors, a dozen of them, angled so that a bird landing sees itself on every side. In the middle, a dish of white millet. Through the mirrors, as you come over the trees, you see a phoenix in every direction: a whole flock of your own kind, waiting for you.

choices.text: Look away from the mirrors and fly on

effects.log: It is the hardest thing. A flock of phoenixes, and you have seen so few of your own kind. You fly on with your eyes shut until the pines are behind you. The hunters, in the reeds, are very disappointed.

choices.text: Land, and look at yourself, just once

ok.log: A dozen birds, all you. Your patterns, your five colours, the way you hold your head. So that is what the humans see. You are off the ground before the clap-net falls, and it falls on a dish of millet.

fail.log: You look too long. The net comes down; you tear through it, but not before the hunters have their hands on your tail. You leave a fortune in feathers behind and limp home through the air. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: caught by feather-takers in a ring of mirrors

choices.text: Smash the mirrors, one by one

effects.log: Twelve mirrors face down in the pine needles. The hunters come out of the reeds shouting and you are gone. Bronze mirrors cost money. They will remember you. (-6 health)

events.text: You follow the feathers. From the hunters' camp to a market, from the market to a workshop behind a hill-lord's hall, where a crown-maker sits at a bench under a window with a gilt-bronze crown in a vice and a tray of feathers beside it, sorting them by colour. Some of them are yours. The crown-maker is very skilled, and very old, and hums.

choices.text: Sit in the window so the crown-maker sees whose feathers they are

effects.log: The humming stops. The old crown-maker looks at you for a long time, and at the tray, and puts down the tweezers. "I thought they came from moulting," the crown-maker says at last. "They told me they came from moulting." The crown is finished without your feathers in it.

choices.text: Watch, and learn what they become

effects.log: Each feather is set upright in a little bronze socket on the crown's branches, so that it trembles when the wearer walks. It is beautiful. It will go into a tomb with the lord. You fly away knowing exactly where your feathers end.

events.text: Feather-takers again: the smell of hemp and pine tar and bronze polish in the reeds below your tree. A new crew, or the old one's sons. Lime on the low branches. A decoy pheasant in a cage, crying.

choices.text: Move your roost to a higher tree

effects.log: A higher tree, a colder wind, a long season of carrying sticks. The crew sits in the reeds for a month and catches the decoy's own cousins. (-3 health)

choices.text: Lead them into the marsh and leave them there

ok.log: A flash of colour, always one reed further on. By evening the crew is up to the waist in the marsh, and arguing. They go home and tell everyone the phoenix of this valley is a demon. Good.

fail.log: A clap-net in the reeds that you did not see. You get out of it. Not all of your tail does. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let the decoy pheasant out of its cage first

effects.log: One tug at the bamboo latch and the pheasant is gone into the grass, still crying, out of habit. The crew finds an empty cage and a five-coloured feather on top of it, and is unsettled for days.

events.text: On a hill below your slope at dusk: {npc}, an apprentice from the court music office, alone, with a set of bamboo panpipes in a wooden frame carved like a bird with spread wings. Sixteen pipes, each stopped with beeswax to its note. {He} is playing the old music, the music of the ancient sage-king that the books say called the phoenixes down. {He} has it almost right.

choices.text: Listen until the light goes

effects.log: Almost right. One pipe, the eleventh, is a hair flat; the beeswax has sagged in the summer heat. The rest is the oldest thing you have ever heard humans make. You find your feathers standing up.

choices.text: Fly away. It is not for you; it only claims to be

effects.log: You leave {npc} to the dusk. Behind you the music goes on, almost right, and follows you up the hill like a dog that has not been told to go home.

events.text: {npc} is back on the hill every dusk, playing the old music, with the eleventh pipe still a hair flat. {He} does not know it. Nobody alive knows it; the music office tunes the pipes to each other, and they are all a hair flat together. Only you, perhaps, have heard how it should go.

choices.text: Sing the true note, once, from the tree

mem.note: sang the true note from the tree

effects.log: One note, from the dark of the paulownia, exactly where the eleventh pipe should be. {npc} stops. {He} stands up. {He} looks into the tree and sees nothing, and blows the eleventh pipe, and hears how wrong it is, and sits down very suddenly on the grass.

choices.text: Leave it flat. A human should find it alone

effects.log: You say nothing. {npc} plays it flat all summer. In the autumn {he} goes back to the capital. You hope {he} finds it. You think {he} might.

events.text: Years go by, and {npc} does not stop. Every dusk, on the same hill, the eleventh pipe, warmed in {his} hands, the beeswax scraped and pressed and scraped again, trying to hear once more the note that came out of the tree. {He} has been passed over twice at the music office for being strange. {He} does not seem to mind.

choices.text: Sing it again, one more time, years later

mem.note: sang the note again, years later

effects.log: Once more, from the tree. {npc} does not stop playing this time. {He} matches it, there and then, on the pipe in {his} hands, and plays the whole old music through with the true note in it, and the hill is very quiet afterwards.

choices.text: Let {him} keep looking. The looking is the music now

effects.log: {npc} never quite finds it. {He} comes close, closer than anyone in the music office. {His} students learn the eleventh pipe from {him}, a hair less flat than before. It is how music gets better: one hair at a time, over lives.

events.text: You can speak now, and {npc} is old, and still comes to the hill at dusk with the panpipes in their phoenix frame. You land on the grass in front of {him}, the first time in all these years, and {he} lowers the pipes and says, before you can say anything, "It was you. The eleventh. It was always you."

choices.text: "It was you that kept listening." Tell {him} the note in words

effects.log: There are no words for a note. You try anyway, and {npc} listens with {his} eyes closed, and nods, and puts the pipe to {his} lips. One note. Exactly. The music office will play it right for a hundred years, and never know who tuned it.

choices.text: Ask {him} to play the whole old music for you, once

effects.log: The nine parts of it, on a hill, at dusk, for one bird. At the last part you find yourself standing, and turning, in the old measured dance, on the grass. {npc} sees it and does not stop playing, and weeps, and does not stop playing.

events.text: You are flying home in the dark over a sleeping village, very low, tired, not looking where you are going, and you fly into a dream. You did not know that could happen. It is a warm dream, red and gold, of a woman expecting a child, sitting in a field at sunrise. You are suddenly in it: a phoenix, coming down out of five-coloured clouds, straight into her arms.

choices.text: Stay a moment, since you are here

effects.log: You fold your wings in the dream and let her hold you. She is laughing. Then you are back over the village in the cold, flying, and in one of the houses below a woman wakes and sits up and says, "A phoenix," to the dark.

choices.text: Back out of the dream as fast as you came in

effects.log: You turn in the red-gold air and go out the way you came. Too late: she has seen five colours. Below, a lamp comes on. The whole house is awake by cockcrow.

events.text: The house you flew through is in uproar. A phoenix in a conception dream is the best dream there is; everybody agrees. Nobody agrees on anything else. The grandmother says a bong means a boy and a hwang a girl, and the dream was obviously a bong. The aunt says hwang. The father says it was two birds. The dreamer, {npc}, says nothing, and smiles, and will not tell.

choices.text: Fly over the house at dawn, once, so they know the dream was real

effects.log: One pass over the roof at sunrise. The whole household out in the yard in nightclothes, pointing. "Bong!" "Hwang!" They are still arguing when the child is born, and for a good while after.

choices.text: Let the dream stay a dream

effects.log: You keep away from that village. A dream should not be checked. {npc} tells the child about it every night for years, and it gets better every time.

events.text: Years after the dream. {npc}, the child of it, has grown up hearing about the phoenix every night of {his} childhood, and is sick of it. Everyone expects great things. {He} climbs the slope to your tree, very angry, and shouts up into the branches: "I am not anything! I am an ordinary person! Was it even you?"

choices.text: Come down to the lowest branch and look at {him}

mem.note: came down and looked at me

effects.log: You look at {npc} for a long time. You do not say anything; you cannot yet. {He} stops shouting. {He} sits down under the tree and says, much quieter, "I suppose ordinary is allowed." You think it very much is.

choices.text: Stay hidden. The dream was {his} parent's, not {his} burden

effects.log: {npc} shouts until hoarse, and then sits under the tree until the sun goes down. Nothing comes. {He} goes home lighter, oddly, as if the bird had agreed.

events.text: The paulownia where your mate last sat. The branch is still bent a little, the way it bent under their weight. There is one of their feathers caught in the twigs, a long one, red at the root. You land beside it and do not know how to leave.

choices.text: Stay on the branch

effects.log: You stay. The days go by on either side of you. The feather moves in the wind and you watch it move. (-4 health)

choices.text: Sing your half of the song, and wait in the stop

effects.log: Your half, and the stop, and nothing. The eleven ranges send your half back to you. They have nothing to put in the stop either.

choices.text: Take the feather, and fly, anywhere

effects.log: You carry the feather a hundred li and put it in a strange tree and sit beside it. It is the same. You knew it would be.

events.text: A year of not eating. Not a vow; you simply do not. The store is under the bark and you do not go to it. Your feathers dull. Hunters see you from the road, because a bird that does not care is easy to see. A sparrow lands on the branch, looks at you, and for once has nothing to say.

choices.text: Go on not eating

effects.log: Another season. You are very light now. When the wind blows you hold on to the branch with both feet, and you are not sure why you hold on. (-14 health)

choices.text: Eat one seed, for the sparrow's sake

effects.log: One seed. The sparrow watches you swallow it and nods, and goes away, satisfied, as if it had done a day's work. Perhaps it had.

choices.text: Fly to the sweet spring, and drink, and come back

effects.log: Water, and the cold of it all the way down. It does not help. It does not hurt either. You come back to the branch. (-6 health)

events.text: A clear night, and the full moon comes up over the ridge and hangs on the end of the empty branch, exactly where your mate used to sit. Below, a poor scholar walking home from the village schoolhouse stops on the road and looks up at the tree for a long time: a bird, a branch, the moon. In the morning, you will learn later, the scholar wrote three lines about it.

choices.text: Let the moon sit there. It is the only one who comes

effects.log: The moon on the empty branch. You sit at the other end. In the village, the scholar's three lines go from the schoolhouse to the market to the capital. Every child will learn them. None of them will know they are about you.

choices.text: Move to the end of the branch, where they sat

effects.log: You sit where they sat, with the moon behind you. From the road it looks like one bird and one moon. The scholar writes that too.

events.text: Dawn on the high ridge, where you first sang and were first answered. You have come here without deciding to. The eleven ranges are grey. Your throat is full of the song, both halves of it now, because there is nobody else to sing the other one.

choices.text: Sing both halves, and make the vow: to go on, for both

effects.log: Your half, and then theirs, in the stop, in your own voice, a little wrong. Then the vow, which has no words, only a turn of the song at the end that was never in it before. The lone song goes out three valleys. A widow at her loom stops and listens. (The Lone Vow.)

choices.text: Sing your half only, and leave the stop empty for them

effects.log: Your half. The stop. Nothing in it. You cannot yet. Perhaps another year. (The vow is still unmade; the high ridge will be here.)

choices.text: Do not sing. Go back to the empty branch

effects.log: You fly back to the branch and the moon. Not yet. Maybe not ever. (-5 health)

events.text: Years alone, and the vow kept. You sing both halves on the high ridge every dawn now, and you have got good at it: the stop in the middle is filled, in your own voice, turned round, the way they used to turn it. The farmers below say there are still two birds on the ridge. You do not correct them.

choices.text: Let them believe it

effects.log: Two birds on the ridge, the farmers say, and set their day by it. In a way, there are.

choices.text: Fly over the paddies once, alone, so they know

effects.log: One bird. The farmers look up and see it and understand, and take off their hats, all down the valley, one paddy after another, like a wind in the rice.

events.text: Dawn in an outer courtyard of the palace, before the officials come. {npc}, an old servant who has swept these flagstones for forty years, looks up from the broom and sees you on the wall, close enough to touch, and does not drop the broom. "So," {he} says. "You are real. Have you come for the throne, then? Everybody will want to know." It is the first time a human has spoken to you expecting an answer, and you find you can give one.

choices.text: "I have come to look. Nothing more, yet."

mem.note: spoke to me in the courtyard

effects.log: {npc} nods, as if this were the most sensible thing a bird ever said, and goes back to sweeping. "Look at the kitchens," {he} says, without turning round. "Thrones lie. Kitchens cannot afford to."

choices.text: "What do you think? You have swept here forty years."

effects.log: Nobody has asked {npc} an opinion in forty years. {He} leans on the broom and gives it, slowly, at length, with names. It is the best report on the court you will ever hear, and it is from a servant with a broom.

choices.text: Say nothing, and fly

effects.log: {npc} watches you go. Then {he} sweeps the place on the wall where you sat, very carefully, and tells no one, and is the happiest servant in the palace for a month.

events.text: Night, a temple roof across from the palace. A figure in plain clothes climbs the temple steps alone, with no lamp, and stops below you, and you know before {he} speaks who it is: {npc}, who holds the land below, out without a single guard. "They say you watch us," says {npc}. "Tell me, then. Am I worthy? I would rather hear it from you than from heaven later."

choices.text: "I do not know yet. Neither do you. That is in your favour."

effects.log: {npc} laughs, short and surprised, and sits down on the temple step. "Nobody has told me they do not know for three years," {he} says. You talk until the bell for the first watch.

choices.text: Tell {him} what you saw at the granary gate at night

mem.note: told me about the night carts

ok.log: {npc} goes white, then red, then very still. The next week a minister is removed and the granary gate is sealed at dusk. A ruler can be told. Not every ruler; this one.

fail.log: {npc} hears it and does not believe it, or cannot afford to. "My ministers are loyal," {he} says, and goes down the steps. Next week there are archers on the temple roofs. You leave the capital for a season.

choices.text: "A phoenix does not tell. It comes, or it does not."

effects.log: {npc} stands on the step a long time. "Then I will have to find out the way everybody else does," {he} says. "By what happens." Yes.

events.text: {npc}, a child from the palace kitchens, has found you on the woodshed roof and climbed up after you with a bowl of millet, warm, the best in the kitchen, stolen at some risk. "You must be hungry," says {npc}. "Everyone says birds are always hungry."

choices.text: "Thank you. I eat only bamboo seed. Keep it for yourself."

effects.log: {npc} eats the millet there and then, sitting next to you on the roof, swinging both legs, and tells you everything about the kitchens: who steals, who is kind, which cook cries at night. It is a better report than any minister's.

choices.text: Take one grain, so the gift is not refused

effects.log: One grain. {npc} watches you swallow it with enormous seriousness, and then climbs down and tells nobody, ever, for the rest of a long life, that the phoenix ate from {his} bowl. (-2 purity)

events.text: {npc}, a minister in fine silk, has worked out where you sit when you watch the palace, and comes up to the roof of the music office by a ladder, puffing. {He} has a proposal. The ruler needs heaven's sign this year: there are rumours, a bad harvest, a restless north. Come in the dance at the spring feast. In return: a paulownia grove, planted and guarded for ever, and a sweet spring walled for you alone.

choices.text: "I come for a worthy ruler, or I do not come. I am not for hire."

effects.log: {npc} goes down the ladder much faster than up. That night the ruler hears from {him} that the phoenix is an omen of rebellion. You did not expect a minister to be honest. You did not expect quite so little.

choices.text: "Plant the grove anyway. Then we will see."

effects.log: {npc} plants a paulownia grove on a hill outside the capital, expecting a sign. You come to the grove and never to the courtyard. The grove is lovely. {npc} is furious for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Ask {him} why the ruler needs a sign so badly this year

effects.log: Because of the harvest, {npc} says, and the north, and then, sweating, a few more things {he} should not have said. You fly off knowing more about this reign than three seasons of watching had told you.

events.text: {npc}, a herald of the court, finds you by the palace pond. The herald's office writes down every omen of the reign: a white deer, a double-eared stalk of rice, a phoenix. They are paid by the omen. {He} has a brush, an inkstone and a very hopeful face. "Only tell me what to write," {he} says. "I will write it beautifully."

choices.text: "Write: the phoenix was seen by a herald, and said nothing."

effects.log: {npc} writes exactly that, and the record office files it, and three hundred years later a scholar finds it and laughs for a whole afternoon.

choices.text: "Write nothing. A seen phoenix is not a blessing yet."

effects.log: {npc} puts the brush away, slowly. "Then I will not be paid," {he} says. "No," you say. {He} sighs, and thinks, and decides {he} would rather have met you than be paid, and is right.

events.text: In the prison yard, outside the west wall, a prisoner at the barred window sees you in the persimmon tree and calls up in a cracked voice. {npc} was a county clerk; {he} wrote down a minister's grain in the wrong column, the honest one. "Bird," says {npc}. "If you go down into that courtyard for this ruler, remember me. That is all. Just remember there was a clerk."

choices.text: "I will remember. It will count."

effects.log: {npc} laughs, which turns into a cough. "That is more than the court gave me," {he} says. You keep the name. Phoenixes, you discover, have long memories for clerks.

choices.text: "Tell me which minister, and which grain."

effects.log: {npc} tells you everything, quickly, in a whisper, with dates. The guard comes before {he} finishes. You fly off with the half of it, and a sour feeling about the granary gate.

events.text: {npc}, a fortune-teller with a stall in the capital market, is selling phoenix feathers: pheasant tail feathers, dyed in five colours, three for a string of cash. {He} has a crowd. You land on the stall's awning, and the crowd looks up, and {npc} looks up, and goes the colour of {his} dye.

choices.text: "Those are pheasant. Tell them."

effects.log: {npc} tells them. There is not a lot else to do with a phoenix on the awning. The crowd demands its cash back and {npc} pays it, and you fly off, and {he} sells the rest of the feathers that afternoon as "touched by the phoenix," at double.

choices.text: Drop one real feather on the stall, and fly

effects.log: One long feather, red at the root, onto the pheasant feathers. Nobody can tell which it is. {npc} can. {He} closes the stall, and goes home, and never sells another feather, and keeps that one in a box.

events.text: {npc}, an old scholar, lives in a two-room house outside the capital with a paulownia in the yard that {he} planted fifty years ago to call the phoenix. It never came. {He} is sitting under it with a cup of barley tea when you land on the wall. {He} looks at you for a long time and says, very politely, "You are late."

choices.text: "I am. I am sorry. Tell me about the tree."

mem.note: came to my tree at last

effects.log: {npc} tells you: the year it was planted, the storm that split it, the poem {he} wrote about the empty branch that every child in the county knows. You listen to all of it, on the wall, and at the end you fly into the tree, and sit in it, and {npc} closes {his} eyes.

choices.text: "Why call a phoenix? What did you want to see?"

effects.log: "Peace," {npc} says. "Proof of it. That it was possible in my lifetime." {He} looks at you. "Is it?" You do not know. You tell {him} so. {He} nods and pours you a cup of barley tea that you do not drink, and the two of you sit with it until dark.

events.text: {npc}, a peddler of combs and needles, has stopped under your tree on the road out of the capital, and noticed you, and decided, as peddlers do, that the polite thing is to make conversation. "Settle something for me," says {npc}. "Bong or hwang? My cousin says hwang. The innkeeper says bong, and the two of them have not spoken since the spring. Which are you?"

choices.text: "Yes."

effects.log: {npc} stares at you for a long moment. Then {he} laughs so hard {he} has to sit down on the comb box, and tells the story at every inn on the road for years, and nobody ever settles anything.

choices.text: "Half of a name. The other half is not here to ask."

mem.note: said it was half a name

effects.log: {npc} looks up the tree as if expecting the other half to be sitting further up, and it is, and the peddler goes very quiet, and picks up the comb box, and bows to the tree, twice.

choices.text: Say nothing; it is not the innkeeper's business

effects.log: {npc} waits, then shrugs, and goes on down the road. "Hwang, then," {he} says over {his} shoulder. "A bong would have answered. Wait till I tell my cousin." You decide not to rise to it.

events.text: {npc}, a court musician, the second flute of the palace orchestra, finds you by the music office at dusk. The second flute is a hair sharp, and has been for years, and nobody else hears it. {He} has stopped sleeping. "You hear it," says {npc}. "I saw you flinch on the roof at the feast. Tell me I am not mad."

choices.text: "You are not mad. Shave the mouth-hole, a hair, toward you."

effects.log: A knife, a hair of bamboo, a breath. The flute is true. {npc} plays one long note into the dusk and starts to weep, and does not stop playing. At the next feast the whole orchestra sounds different, and nobody can say why.

choices.text: "Why does it matter so much to you?"

effects.log: "Because the music is the reign," {npc} says. "The old books say so. If the music is false, the court is false." A pause. "And because the flute is mine." You like {him} for the second reason more than the first.
